quote: A single arbitrary unit representing the magnitude of global TL for each session is then calculated by the multiplication of training intensity and the length of training (mins). Example: for a session of 87 min, with RPE of 4 (quite hard), the calculations: 87 × 4 will provide a TL of 348 A.U.
claim: Session-RPE training load = session RPE on the modified CR-10 scale (asked after the session: 'How was your workout?') multiplied by session duration in minutes, in arbitrary units; e.g. 87 min at RPE 4 = 348 AU.
population: athletes of all ages and sports (method description)

quote: 36 studies have examined the validity and reliability of this proposed method using the modified CR-10. ... These studies confirmed the validity and good reliability and internal consistency of session-RPE method in several sports and physical activities with men and women of different age categories
claim: Session-RPE has been examined for validity and reliability in 36 studies and shows good validity, reliability and internal consistency across sports, sexes, ages and expertise levels, so it is usable as a mode-independent internal-load measure (strength, running, cycling, climbing).
population: men and women, children to adults, multiple sports
used_for: choosing sRPE as the default internal-load metric
caveat: Narrative mini-review; validity is mostly correlation with HR-based TRIMP in endurance and team sports, with fewer data for resistance training or climbing.

quote: Where weekly mean TL is the average daily TL during the week and SD is the standard deviation of the daily TL calculated over a week. ... This variable is equal to the multiplication of the weekly TL and the monotony scores. ... This type of training has been associated with incidence of illness and poor performance
claim: Training monotony = mean daily load over a week divided by the standard deviation of daily load; training strain = weekly load multiplied by monotony. High load with little day-to-day variation (high strain) has been associated with illness and poor performance.
population: athletes monitored with sRPE (original work by Foster in experienced athletes)
caveat: Thresholds were individually identified in small samples (Foster 1998, N=25); use monotony/strain as a prompt to vary hard and easy days, not as a validated predictor.

quote: No single marker has been validated to identify when an athlete has entered a maladaptive state; hence, it is recommended to use a combination of external and internal load measures that are relevant and specific to the nature of each sport.
claim: No single marker identifies maladaptation; monitor a combination of external load (distance, duration, power) and internal load (sRPE, HR) that fits the sport.
used_for: which metrics to combine in a weekly analysis

quote: Athletes respond significantly better to relatively small increases (and decreases), rather than larger fluctuations in loading. ... Load should always be prescribed on an individual and flexible basis, as there is large intra- and inter-individual variation in the timeframe of response and adaptation to load.
claim: Progress load in small steps rather than large fluctuations, and individualise load because response and adaptation vary widely within and between athletes.
population: athletes; evidence mainly from team sports and cricket

quote: athletes should limit weekly increases of their training load to less than 10%, or maintain an acute:chronic load ... ratio within a range of 0.8 to 1.3, to stay in positive adaptation and thus reduce the risk of injuries
claim: The 2016 IOC consensus advised keeping weekly load increases below 10% or an acute:chronic load ratio of 0.8-1.3 to reduce injury risk.
population: Australian football, cricket and rugby league athletes
used_for: historical ACWR threshold (do not use as a predictor)
caveat: Later critiques showed the 0.8-1.3 'sweet spot' model was illustrative and methodologically flawed (Impellizzeri2020b); an RCT of a 10% rule in novice runners found no benefit (Buist2008).

quote: Training-load measures cannot tell us whether the variations are increasing or decreasing the injury risk; we recommend that practitioners still rely on their expert knowledge and experience.
claim: Training-load metrics (acute load, chronic load, ACWR) cannot tell whether a given load change raises or lowers injury risk; load progression remains a judgement based on training principles and the athlete's response.
used_for: not using ACWR thresholds as injury predictors

quote: observed that the ACWR failed to normalize the numerator for the denominator even after controlling for the mathematical coupling. ... This failure adds unnecessary “noise,” increases the risk of artifact, ... and makes the results difficult to interpret, as the practitioner cannot determine whether the acute or chronic TL is driving the ACWR.
claim: The ACWR is a ratio that does not normalise acute load for chronic load (even when uncoupled), which adds noise and artefacts; a high ACWR cannot show whether it reflects a jump in acute load or a low chronic base.
used_for: explaining ACWR limitations to a coach

quote: Elevated ACWR showed a small-to-moderate association with higher injury risk (g = 0.35; 95% CI, 0.16-0.54), with substantial heterogeneity (I2 = 95.8%).
claim: In a 2026 multilevel meta-analysis, elevated ACWR had a small-to-moderate association with injury (g = 0.35) but with very high heterogeneity (I2 = 95.8%).

quote: current evidence does not support its use as a stand-alone causal or predictive model. ACWR should be interpreted as a contextual monitoring indicator within individualized, multi-marker load-management systems.
claim: ACWR should not be used as a stand-alone causal or predictive injury model; at most it is one contextual indicator among several.
used_for: not using ACWR thresholds as injury predictors

quote: 'small spike' between >10% and 30% increase; (3) 'moderate spike' between >30% and 100% increase; and (4) 'large spike' >100% increase. ... Significantly increased rates were identified for small spikes (HRR=1.64 (95% CI: 1.31 to 2.05, p=0.01)), moderate spikes (HRR=1.52 (95% CI: 1.16 to 2.00, p<0.01)) and large spikes (HRR=2.28 (95% CI: 1.50 to 3.48, p<0.01))
claim: When a single run was longer than the longest run of the previous 30 days by >10-30%, >30-100% or >100%, the overuse-injury rate was 1.64, 1.52 and 2.28 times that of runs up to 10% longer.
population: 5205 adult recreational runners (mean age 45.8, 22% female), Garmin data
used_for: single-session distance spike rule for runners
caveat: Observational cohort with self-reported injuries; association, not proven causation. The authors add that progressions up to 10% also carry some risk and that several consecutive increases within one week may still be excessive.

quote: A negative dose-response relationship was observed for the ACWR. No relationship was identified for the week-to-week ratio.
claim: In the same runner cohort, week-level ACWR showed a negative dose-response with injury and week-to-week change showed no relationship; the single-session spike was the informative signal.
used_for: why weekly ratios are not used as injury flags for runners

quote: The graded 13-week training program was based on the 10% training rule. ... The incidence of RRI was 20.8% in the graded training program group and 20.3% in the standard training program group.
claim: An RCT of a graded 13-week programme following the 10% rule found the same running-injury incidence as a standard 8-week programme (20.8% vs 20.3%).
population: 532 novice runners preparing for a 6.7 km event

quote: Seven studies (87.5%) carried out daily HRV assessments in the morning after awakening ... Five studies (62.5%) used RMSSD as the vagal-related HRV index to guide training ... of which, three used a 7-day averaged HRV value ... Three studies (37.5%) calculated the reference criterion as mean − (1·SD) [19,21,22], three (37.5%) as mean ± (0.5·SD)
claim: HRV-guided training studies mostly measured HRV each morning after waking and mostly used RMSSD; several used a 7-day rolling average, and the individual reference band was usually baseline mean minus 1 SD or mean plus/minus 0.5 SD.
number: 87.5% morning; 62.5% RMSSD; 7-day average; mean - 1 SD or mean +/- 0.5 SD
population: 8 HRV-guided training studies (sedentary to high-level endurance athletes)
caveat: Recording position and averaging method varied between studies; which protocol is best is untested.

quote: HRV-guided training was superior for enhancing vagal-related HRV indices (SMD+ = 0.50 (95% confidence interval (CI) = 0.09, 0.91)), but not resting HR (SMD+ = 0.04 (95% CI = -0.34, 0.43)). Consistently small but non-significant (p > 0.05) SMDs in favor of HRV-guided training were observed for enhancing maximal aerobic capacity (SMD+ = 0.20
claim: Compared with predefined training, HRV-guided training improved vagal HRV (SMD 0.50) but gave only small, non-significant advantages for maximal aerobic capacity (SMD 0.20) and no difference for resting HR.
number: SMD 0.50 (0.09-0.91) vagal HRV; 0.04 resting HR; 0.20 maximal aerobic capacity
population: 199 participants in 8 studies, mostly endurance-trained or active adults

quote: HRV-guided training may be more effective than predefined training for maintaining and improving vagal-mediated HRV, with less likelihood of negative responses. However, if HRV-guided training is superior to predefined training for producing group-level improvements in fitness and performance, current data suggest it is only by a small margin.
claim: HRV-guided training may reduce the chance of negative responses, but any group-level fitness or performance advantage over a well-designed fixed plan is small.

quote: This results in reduced HRV concurrent with reduced resting HR due to saturation of myocardial cholinergic receptors from parasympathetic predominance
claim: In highly trained athletes, a low HRV together with a low resting HR can reflect parasympathetic saturation, not fatigue, which would mislead a simple HRV rule.

quote: Subjective and objective measures of athlete well-being generally did not correlate. Subjective measures reflected acute and chronic training loads with superior sensitivity and consistency than objective measures.
claim: Self-reported well-being responds to acute and chronic training load more sensitively and consistently than objective markers (blood markers, HR), and the two generally do not correlate.
population: athletes in 56 studies with concurrent measures
used_for: prioritising check-in answers over device markers

quote: To monitor acute changes in athlete well-being, the following subscales may be useful: vigour/motivation, physical symptoms/injury, non-training stress, fatigue, physical recovery, general health/well-being, and being in shape.
claim: Useful check-in items for acute changes: motivation/vigour, physical symptoms or injury, non-training stress, fatigue, physical recovery, general health/well-being and feeling in shape.

quote: This may be avoided by having athletes compare their current well-being to normal (ie, worse than normal, normal, better than normal) as in the DALDA.
claim: Ask athletes to rate each item relative to their normal (worse than normal, normal, better than normal), which avoids needing a long baseline for absolute scores.

quote: previous recommendations for daily monitoring using a measure self-administered by the athlete remain appropriate.1 3–6 8 89 92 93 This may be supplemented with a more comprehensive measure such as the POMS or RESTQ-S on a weekly basis
claim: Use a brief daily self-report, optionally supplemented by a longer questionnaire weekly and objective measures less often (about once per training microcycle).

quote: Heart rate measurements for example were associated with error rates of approximately − 3.39 bpm [36], or ± 3% [15], contingent upon user characteristics (e.g. skin tone), intensities of exercise and types of activities and device models
claim: Wrist wearables measure heart rate with errors of roughly -3.4 bpm or plus/minus 3% on average, but error depends on skin tone, exercise intensity, activity type and device.
population: healthy adults in validation studies (umbrella of 6 reviews)

quote: the results of the subgroup meta-analyses for different intensities and types of activities revealed an underestimation of heart rate for cycling activities compared with daily living and treadmill activities as well as overground walking
claim: Wrist-based HR (Fitbit meta-analysis) underestimated heart rate more during cycling than during walking or treadmill activity, so cyclists' wrist HR is less trustworthy than a chest strap.
caveat: Data are from one manufacturer; the chest-strap recommendation is an inference from chest straps being used as the criterion.

quote: the available research evaluating heart rate variability showed a high level of accuracy in rest measurements, with strong agreement with criterion measures, but this deteriorated during periods of physical exercise or motion
claim: Wearable HRV is accurate at rest but degrades during exercise or movement, so use resting (morning or overnight) HRV, not HRV recorded during exercise.

quote: energy expenditure (mean bias = - 3 kcal per minute, or - 3%, with error ranging from - 21.27 to 14.76%)
claim: Wearable energy-expenditure estimates are on average slightly low, but errors range from about -21% to +15%, so treat watch calorie figures as rough estimates.

quote: Sleep measurement showed a tendency to overestimate total sleep time (mean absolute percentage error typically > 10%).
claim: Consumer sleep trackers tend to overestimate total sleep time, with errors typically above 10% versus polysomnography.

quote: wearables using resting condition information in their algorithms significantly overestimated VO2max (bias 2.17 ml·kg-1·min-1; limits of agreement - 13.07 to 17.41 ml·kg-1·min-1), while devices using exercise-based information in their algorithms showed a lower systematic and random error (bias - 0.09 ml·kg-1·min-1; limits of agreement - 9.92 to 9.74 ml·kg-1·min-1)
claim: Wearable VO2max from resting algorithms overestimates (bias +2.17, limits of agreement -13.07 to +17.41 ml/kg/min); exercise-based algorithms (e.g. from runs with HR) are unbiased on average but individual limits of agreement are still about plus/minus 10 ml/kg/min.
number: resting: bias 2.17 (LoA -13.07 to 17.41); exercise: bias -0.09 (LoA -9.92 to 9.74) ml/kg/min

quote: Active recovery, massage, compression garments, immersion, contrast water therapy, and cryotherapy induced a small to large decrease (-2.26 < g < -0.40) in the magnitude of DOMS, while there was no change for the other methods. Massage was found to be the most powerful technique for recovering from DOMS and fatigue.
claim: Active recovery, massage, compression garments, water immersion, contrast water therapy and cryotherapy reduce muscle soreness (g -0.40 to -2.26); massage was the most effective for soreness and perceived fatigue.
population: 99 studies, mostly healthy young adults after exercise
caveat: Outcomes are soreness, fatigue ratings and blood markers, not performance or long-term adaptation.

quote: Post-rolling slightly attenuated exercise-induced decreases in sprint (+3.1%, g = 0.34) and strength performance (+3.9 %, g = 0.21). It also reduced muscle pain perception (+6.0%, g = 0.47)
claim: Foam rolling after exercise gives small benefits: slightly less loss of sprint (g = 0.34) and strength (g = 0.21) performance and less perceived muscle pain (g = 0.47).
number: sprint g 0.34; strength g 0.21; pain g 0.47
used_for: foam rolling as an optional recovery tool

quote: The primary analysis conducted on comparative effect sizes provided some evidence of greater relative hypertrophic adaptations with RT compared to CWI + RT (cSMD0.5 = −0.22 [95% CrI: −0.47 to 0.04]) ... the application of CWI immediately following bouts of RT may attenuate hypertrophic changes.
claim: Cold-water immersion immediately after resistance training probably blunts muscle growth (comparative SMD -0.22 versus training alone); avoid it after sessions whose goal is hypertrophy.
caveat: Fair-to-poor study quality; credible interval crosses zero slightly.

quote: Adults should sleep 7 or more hours per night on a regular basis to promote optimal health.
claim: Adults should regularly sleep 7 or more hours per night.

quote: Children 6 to 12 years of age should sleep 9 to 12 hours per 24 hours on a regular basis to promote optimal health. Teenagers 13 to 18 years of age should sleep 8 to 10 hours per 24 hours on a regular basis to promote optimal health.
claim: Children aged 6-12 should sleep 9-12 hours and teenagers aged 13-18 should sleep 8-10 hours per 24 hours.

quote: A one-size-fits-all approach to athlete sleep recommendations (eg, 7-9 hours/night) is unlikely ideal for health and performance. We recommend an individualised approach that should consider the athlete's perceived sleep needs.
claim: A fixed 7-9 h target is unlikely ideal for every athlete; individualise using the athlete's perceived sleep need.

quote: Even short naps of <30 min can enhance mood, alertness and cognitive performance in those who get sufficient ... Time naps from 13:00 to 16:00 hours when there is a dip in alertness
claim: Naps of under 30 minutes, timed between 13:00 and 16:00, can improve mood, alertness and cognitive performance and can supplement short night sleep.

quote: a small group of trained cyclists and triathletes, showed better endurance performance after three consecutive nights of sleep extension (~8.4 hours sleep each night) compared with habitual sleep (~6.8 hours sleep each night)
claim: In a small study of trained cyclists and triathletes, three nights of sleep extension (about 8.4 h vs 6.8 h habitual) improved endurance performance; sleep extension or banking is plausible but weakly evidenced.
population: small group of trained cyclists and triathletes
caveat: Authors caution that most sleep-extension studies lack control groups.

quote: refer athletes to a sleep specialist for clinical diagnosis, when necessary (figure 2 and table 1). This is an important step because any sleep-focused strategies will likely be ineffective in the presence of untreated sleep disorders.
claim: Screen for sleep problems and refer to a sleep specialist when a disorder is suspected, because sleep-hygiene strategies are unlikely to work while a sleep disorder is untreated.
used_for: referral trigger for persistent sleep problems

quote: Investigations measuring exercise performance under 'control' (i.e., normal sleep, > 6 h in any 24 h period) and 'intervention' (i.e., sleep loss, ≤ 6 h sleep in any 24 h period) conditions were included. ... (n = 959 [89%] male; mean %Δ = - 7.56%, 95% CI - 11.9 to - 3.13, p = 0.001, I2 = 98.1%)
claim: Acute sleep loss (6 h or less in 24 h) reduced exercise performance by about 7.6% on average across strength, endurance, power and skill tasks.
used_for: adjusting the session after a short night

quote: A significant positive relationship was observed between time awake prior to the exercise task and %Δ in performance for both deprivation and late-restriction protocols (~ 0.4% decrease for every hour awake prior to exercise). The negative effects of sleep loss on different exercise tasks performed in the PM were consistent, while tasks performed in the AM were largely unaffected.
claim: After sleep loss, performance falls about 0.4% per hour awake before exercise; evening sessions were consistently impaired while morning sessions were largely unaffected.
used_for: scheduling hard sessions after sleep loss

quote: Stratified exposure analyses proved no beneficial effect for stretching (RR 0.963 (0.846-1.095)), whereas studies with multiple exposures (RR 0.655 (0.520-0.826)), proprioception training (RR 0.550 (0.347-0.869)), and strength training (RR 0.315 (0.207-0.480)) showed a tendency towards increasing effect.
claim: Exercise-based injury prevention works, except stretching (RR 0.96, no effect); strength training had the largest effect (RR 0.32), proprioception RR 0.55, multi-component programmes RR 0.66.
number: stretching RR 0.963; multiple RR 0.655; proprioception RR 0.550; strength RR 0.315
population: 25 RCTs, 26 610 participants, mostly team and youth sport

quote: Cluster-adjusted intention-to-treat analysis established RR 0.338 (0.238-0.480). The result was consistent across robustness tests and strength of evidence was high. A 10% increase in strength training volume reduced the risk of injury by more than four percentage points.
claim: Strength-training-based prevention cut sports injuries to about one third (RR 0.34), and a 10% increase in strength-training volume reduced injury risk by more than 4 percentage points.
used_for: including strength work in every plan

quote: There is a reduction in the overall injury risk ratio of 0.49 (95% CI 0.32 to 0.74, p=0.0008) in favour of programmes including the NHE.
claim: Programmes including the Nordic hamstring exercise roughly halve hamstring injuries (risk ratio 0.49).
used_for: hamstring injury prevention for sprint/field and running athletes

quote: Overall pooled results showed no significant differences between intervention and control groups in injury risk (z = - 1.60; p = 0.110) and injury rate (z = - 0.98; p = 0.329), while a post hoc analysis evaluating supervised interventions only showed that injury risk was significantly lower in the intervention group
claim: In endurance runners, exercise-based prevention programmes did not significantly reduce running injuries overall; only supervised programmes (post hoc) showed lower injury risk.
population: 1904 endurance runners in 9 RCTs (7 low quality)
caveat: Contrasts with large benefits in team and youth sports (Lauersen2014, Lauersen2018); compliance may explain the difference.

quote: Overall, the certainty of the evidence determining whether different types of running shoes influence running injury rates was very low to low, and as such we are uncertain as to the true effects of different types of running shoes upon injury rates. There is no evidence that prescribing footwear based on foot type reduces running-related lower-limb injures in adults.
claim: No running-shoe type (neutral/cushioned, minimalist, motion control, stability, soft or hard midsole) has been shown to change running-injury rates (very low to low certainty), and there is no evidence that prescribing shoes by foot type reduces injuries (moderate certainty, military recruits).
population: adult runners and military recruits, 12 trials, 11 240 participants

quote: there is little research available to support a sound scientific approach to RTS after an ARinf. Historically, RTS decisions following an ARinf were guided by expert ... opinion to follow the “neck check” rule.
claim: The 'neck check' rule for training with a respiratory infection is historical expert opinion with little research behind it; the IOC replaced it with a symptom-based, stepwise process.

quote: Question 1: Do you have any of the following symptoms at rest? Fever (raised body temperature) Chills Excessive fatigue / tiredness General muscle aches and pains Breathing difficulty, including fast breathing or shortness of breath Chest pain, chest pressure, or chest tightness Dizziness, palpitations / racing heart (faster than normal) at rest
claim: Before resuming training after a respiratory infection, the athlete answers a daily checklist; any symptom at rest such as fever, chills, excessive fatigue, body aches, breathing difficulty, chest pain or tightness, dizziness or palpitations means no exercise test yet.
population: athletes with mild or asymptomatic acute respiratory infection

quote: Choose a moderate exercise intensity (60-70% of normal exercise intensity) ... Assess your response (how you feel) after 10-20min of exercise ... Monitor for symptoms during exercise ... immediately after exercise and 24 hours after exercise
claim: If the checklist is clear, do a self-administered exercise challenge at 60-70% of normal intensity for 10-20 minutes and monitor symptoms during and for 24 hours after.
population: athletes with mild or asymptomatic acute respiratory infection

quote: Discontinue the exercise challenge test if any of the following symptoms develop during exercise (excessive fatigue / tiredness, shortness of breath / breathlessness, chest pain / discomfort, dizziness, palpitations / racing heart (faster than normal e.g. on heart rate monitor), muscle / joint pain, higher level of effort for the same past exercise load, and "not feeling well") - consult with a medical doctor if any these symptoms develop
claim: Stop the first session back and consult a doctor if excessive fatigue, breathlessness, chest pain, dizziness, palpitations, muscle or joint pain, unusually high effort for a familiar load, or feeling unwell appear.
population: athletes returning after acute respiratory infection

quote: If there are no abnormal responses during or after exercise, the athlete can progress with increased training load (increased training frequency, intensity, and duration), while self-monitoring for the same abnormal responses during and after each exercise training session
claim: With no abnormal responses to the test session, progress training frequency, intensity and duration step by step while checking for the same symptoms during and after every session.
population: athletes returning after mild or asymptomatic acute respiratory infection

quote: The RTS process for moderate or severe ARinf should be under the care of a physician or other healthcare professional.
claim: Return to sport after a moderate or severe respiratory infection should be managed by a physician or other healthcare professional, not by the coach.
population: athletes with moderate or severe acute respiratory infection

quote: in several larger studies this complication was found to be rare (< 3% or less).(60-62) Thus, although potential complications of ARinf affecting multiple organ systems are rare, the SEM clinician should consider these complications as they may predispose athletes to an increased risk of adverse medical events during return to full training and competition.
claim: Myocarditis or pericarditis after SARS-CoV-2 infection is rare in athletes (under 3% in larger studies), but such complications may raise the risk of adverse events on return to full training, which is why cardiac-type symptoms need medical review.

quote: We conclude that the session RPE method is a valid method of quantitating exercise training during a wide variety of types of exercise.
claim: The original validation study concluded that session RPE (rating times duration) is a valid way to quantify training across steady cycling, interval cycling and basketball practice, compared with a heart-rate-based method.
population: healthy subjects doing cycling and basketball (abstract only; small samples)
caveat: validated against heart rate, not against injury or adaptation; resistance training and climbing were not tested

quote: The findings of this review support the association between the ACWR and non-contact injuries and its use as a valuable tool for monitoring training load as part of a larger scale multifaceted monitoring system that includes other proven methods.
claim: A systematic review of 22 team-sport studies supported an association between ACWR and non-contact injury and endorsed ACWR as one tool inside a wider monitoring system, with the exponentially weighted average version preferred over the rolling average.
caveat: this is the supportive side of a contested area; see MON-53 to MON-56 for the critiques

quote: The majority of studies suggest that athletes are at greater risk of sustaining a time-loss injury when the ACWR is higher relative to a lower or moderate ACWR. The heterogenous methodological approaches not only reflect the wide range of sports studied and the differing demands of these activities, but also limit the strength of recommendations.
claim: A systematic review of professional team-sport studies found most reported higher injury risk at higher ACWR, but the heterogeneous methods limit the strength of any recommendation.
population: adult male professional team-sport athletes (mean age 24 years)
caveat: all studies male and elite; see MON-54

quote: The ACWR was commonly calculated using the coupled method (95%), 1:4 weekly blocks (95%) and subsequent week injury lag (80%). There were 14 different binning methods with almost none of the studies using the same binning categories.
claim: In ACWR injury studies the coupled calculation was used in 95% of studies, and 14 different binning methods were used, which makes thresholds from different studies incomparable.

quote: We argue that no evidence supports the quantitative use of TL data to manipulate future training with the purpose of preventing injury.
claim: Impellizzeri and colleagues argue that no evidence supports using training-load data quantitatively to adjust future training in order to prevent injury.
population: expert commentary on sport and team-sport research
caveat: expert opinion; an argued position, not a meta-analysis

quote: Training load and its associated metrics cannot provide a quantitative indication of whether particular load progressions will increase or decrease the injury risk, given the nature of previous studies (descriptive and at best predictive) and their methodologic weaknesses.
claim: Training-load metrics cannot say whether a particular load progression raises or lowers injury risk, because previous studies were descriptive or at best predictive and methodologically weak; the most appropriate progression comes from expert knowledge, experience and best practice.

quote: HRV measurements acquired from portable devices differed from those obtained from ECG (ES = 0.23, 95% CI 0.05-0.42), although this effect was small and highly heterogeneous
claim: Portable heart-rate-variability devices differed from ECG with a small average error (effect size 0.23) that was highly heterogeneous; the authors judge the error acceptable given better practicality and compliance.
population: 23 studies comparing portable devices with ECG (short recordings, mostly rest)
caveat: most studies were short recordings; overnight or all-day wearable HRV was not the focus

quote: Moderator analysis revealed that HRV metric (p <0.001), position (p = 0.033), and biological sex (β = 0.45, 95% CI 0.30-0.61; p <0.001), but not portable device, modulated the degree of absolute error.
claim: Measurement error depended on the HRV metric, body position and sex, but not on which portable device was used; recordings in the tilt/recovery position had the largest error.
population: 23 studies comparing portable devices with ECG
caveat: keep the same position every day

quote: Fixed effects meta-analysis revealed a significant medium-sized positive effect of HRV-guided training on submaximal physiological parameters (g = 0.296, 95% CI 0.031 to 0.562, p = 0.028), but its effects on performance (g = 0.079, 95% CI -0.050 to 0.393, p = 0.597) and V̇O2peak (g = 0.171, 95% CI -0.213 to 0.371, p = 0.130) were small and not statistically significant.
claim: In a meta-analysis of 8 studies of HRV-guided endurance training with wearables, HRV guidance improved submaximal physiological parameters (g 0.296) but had small, non-significant effects on performance (g 0.079) and VO2peak (g 0.171).
number: submaximal g 0.296; performance g 0.079; VO2peak g 0.171
caveat: small number of studies with different protocols

quote: Compared to predefined training, most HRV-guided interventions included fewer moderate- and/or high-intensity training sessions.
claim: Compared with predefined plans, most HRV-guided interventions contained fewer moderate- and high-intensity sessions, and HRV guidance was associated with fewer non-responders on performance.
caveat: a possible benefit may come from fewer hard sessions rather than from HRV itself

quote: HRV-guided training and control training enhanced the athletes' VO2max (p < 0.0001), but the ES for the HRV-guided training group was significantly higher (p < 0.0001; ESHRVG-CG = 0.187).
claim: A meta-analysis of randomised trials in endurance athletes found a small but significant VO2max advantage for HRV-guided over control training (effect size 0.187), and better results in amateur and female subgroups.
population: trained endurance athletes in RCTs; amateur and female subgroups reported larger gains
caveat: a more careful review (Manresa-Rocamora 2021) found small non-significant effects

quote: Large and significant heterogeneity was observed for many devices (I2 >75%). Combining heart rate or heat sensing technology with accelerometry decreased the error in most activity types.
claim: Wrist and arm-worn energy-expenditure estimates varied greatly in accuracy (heterogeneity above 75%) and by activity type; devices that combined heart rate with accelerometry had smaller errors in most activity types.
population: healthy adults in 60 validation studies (abstract only)
caveat: no pooled error percentage in the abstract; see MON-25 for the range

quote: Protocols of 10-15 min at 10-15 or 5-10 °C appear to be most effective for improving performance and recovery.
claim: If cold-water immersion is used for recovery, 10-15 min at 10-15 degrees C (or 5-10 degrees C) appeared the most effective protocol in an umbrella review.
caveat: low to very low certainty

quote: CWI did not improve muscular strength performance, and impaired strength and hypertrophic gains.
claim: Post-exercise cold-water immersion did not improve strength performance and impaired strength and hypertrophy gains.
caveat: certainty low to very low

quote: Overall methodological quality was low to critically low, and certainty of evidence was low to very low, mainly due to inconsistency and imprecision.
claim: The umbrella review rated the methodological quality of the included cold-water immersion meta-analyses as low to critically low and the certainty of evidence as low to very low, and favours a periodised, context-driven use rather than routine use after every session.
population: 15 systematic reviews with meta-analysis (161 unique studies)
